Unit 01 Reading 1 블루베리는 원래 파란색이 아니라고?
Among the many colorful fruits in shades of red, orange, and yellow, one stands out for its rare color: the blueberry.
Blueberries are among the very few foods that appear blue.
But if you cut one in half and take a closer look, you’ll notice that beneath its blue surface, the skin is actually dark red.
So, how does this little berry manage to look blue?
Whereas blueberries contain a red pigment called anthocyanin, their blue color comes from a powdery coating on their skin, known as bloom.
This coating has tiny, nearly invisible structures — thinner than a sheet of paper — that reflect light in a way that makes the berries appear blue to our eyes.
Researchers hope that blueberries’ natural color effect could inspire new coloring techniques for human use.
They could be used to develop eco-friendly blue coloring for makeup, food, and plastic.
It’s remarkable how such a tiny berry can spark big ideas for a greener future!
Unit 01 Reading 2 팁은 어떻게 미국의 상징이 되었을까?
Tipping in America has a long and complex history.
It began in the 1800s when wealthy Americans traveled to Europe and were influenced by English aristocrats who tipped their servants.
They brought the custom back, and tipping soon became a symbol of wealth and status in American culture.
However, not everyone liked the idea.
Many Americans thought tipping made the workers seem inferior and went against American values of equality.
Critics argued that workers should be paid fair wages without having to hope for customer generosity.
In the early 1900s, some states even passed laws to ban tipping.
Still, tipping gained overwhelming support within the service economy.
Employers welcomed it as a way to cut labor costs, and customers saw it as a tool to improve service quality.
By the 1930s, tipping was written into U.S. labor laws.
Today, tipping has expanded beyond traditional settings.
With touchscreens at cafes and shops, customers are made to tip for even things like takeout and coffee.
This has sparked debates about when tipping is appropriate.
Though it has kept Americans arguing for centuries, tipping remains a unique tradition that refuses to fade away.
Unit 01 Reading 3 왜 아이슬란드 사람들은 아기 새를 절벽에서 던질까?
In late summer or early autumn in Iceland, you might witness an unusual sight: people throwing baby birds off cliffs!
Although this may look brutal, it is actually a thoughtful tradition that helps these young birds begin their first journey.
Puffins are small seabirds beloved as a symbol of Iceland.
They nest on high cliffs, where they care for their chicks, known as pufflings.
When pufflings are ready to leave, they take their first journey at night.
They follow the moonlight to find their way to the sea.
However, the bright lights from towns often confuse them.
Instead of flying to the ocean, they may head toward the city, which can lead to dangerous crashes or falls on buildings, streets, or harbors.
Fortunately, the people of Iceland have a deep affection for puffins.
During the season when pufflings leave their nests, families and rescue teams walk the streets at night in search of lost pufflings.
They carefully bring the birds to the cliffs and give them a gentle toss.
This gives the pufflings, exhausted from failed attempts, the boost they need to take flight.
Once in the air, their wings instinctively flap, and they are carried safely to the ocean.
The annual effort to guide pufflings safely to the sea not only helps conserve these birds but also brings the community together in a festive and meaningful way.
It’s a time of year Icelanders truly treasure.
Unit 02 Reading 1 머리가 없는데 머리라고? 불가사리의 비밀
Sea stars, or starfish, are one of the world’s most unusual marine creatures.
They don’t have a brain, blood, or a distinct head.
For years, their strange biological features have puzzled scientists.
Since sea stars don’t have a visible head, scientists once thought they didn’t have one at all.
To their surprise, however, recent studies indicate the exact opposite.
Most animals, like humans, have bodies divided into two equal halves — a left side and a right side.
In contrast, sea stars have bodies arranged in a circular shape with five equal sections.

When scientists studied the genes of sea stars and compared them to the genes of other animals, they discovered that sea stars have genetic patterns similar to the ones that form the ‘head’ in other animals.
This suggests that, rather than having a head in one part of the body, sea stars distribute head-like functions throughout their entire body.
They don't have a head — they are a head!
This becomes clearer when we observe how sea stars use their body.
Each part — whether a foot, an arm, or a mouth — can sense, process, and respond to information on its own.
For example, when their feet detect something, their feet simultaneously act as independent decision-makers, reacting without help from a distinct head.
These discoveries provide creative examples of how life can evolve, and lead scientists to reconsider what a head truly is.
Unit 02 Reading 2 쉬엄쉬엄 운동해도 효과가 있다고?
How intense are your workouts?
Exercise intensity is typically divided into five zones.
Zone 1 includes very light activities, like slow walking, while Zone 5 involves maximum effort, such as sprinting.
Many assume that high-intensity workouts in Zone 5 produce the best results, but that’s not always true.
Zone 2 training, a low-to-moderate intensity exercise, is one of the best ways to stay healthy and build lasting energy.
Zone 2 exercise happens when your heart rate is 60 to 70 percent of its maximum.
Activities like a fast walk, light jogging, or easy cycling fall into this category.
A simple way to know if you’re working out in Zone 2 is the “talk test” — you should be able to chat comfortably without losing your breath.
It’s a pace you can maintain for a long time, which makes it perfect for anyone wanting a steady, enjoyable workout.
One of Zone 2’s biggest benefits is that it boosts energy use and endurance.
At this level, your body burns fat as its main energy source, which not only helps with weight loss but also enhances stamina.
Zone 2 training also improves heart health by increasing its ability to handle physical activity.
Unlike intense workouts, Zone 2 doesn’t leave you sore or worn out, so you can exercise again the next day.
For a healthier, happier routine, Zone 2 workouts should be just what you need.
Who knew taking it easy could be so powerful?
Unit 02 Reading 3 미로와 래버린스는 어떻게 다를까?
Labyrinths are ancient designs that lead people along a single, winding path to the center and back again.
Unlike mazes, which are meant to confuse and challenge, labyrinths offer a path with no choices to make or dead ends to fear.
They encourage walkers to slow down, reflect, and find a sense of inner peace.
For thousands of years, labyrinths have been a part of human history.
They appeared across different cultures as either decorative forms — such as patterns on tiles or carvings on rocks — or walkable paths on cathedral floors.
These labyrinths played important roles in spiritual and religious rituals.
In prehistoric times, they were used as traps for harmful spirits.
During the medieval period, they served as symbolic journeys for those who couldn’t travel on long pilgrimages.
Today, labyrinths have lost much of their religious purpose and are mainly used to comfort the mind and soul.
They appear as stone paths in parks, floor patterns in hospitals or schools, and even small, portable “finger labyrinths” for tracing by hand.
Many people find labyrinth walking a meaningful way to lower stress, enhance focus, and promote emotional well-being.
It goes without saying that labyrinths carry timeless wisdom that transcends time and culture.
Unit 03 Reading 1 시끄러운 매미가 프로방스의 상징이 된 이유는?
In Provence, France, cicadas are more than just noisy insects.
They’re cherished symbols of the region’s sunny and relaxed spirit.
Each summer, as their chorus fills the warm air, locals and visitors are invited to join the cicadas’ carefree way of life.
They slow down, and enjoy the moment; just as cicadas spend their days bathing in the sun and singing their joyful song.
For centuries, artists and poets in Provence have praised cicadas.
Even when a fable describing the cicada as a lazy creature gained popularity across France, they saw things differently.
The cicada was a symbol of appreciating the present moment.
They saw in these insects a reflection of their own love for music, sunshine, and the art of relaxation.
Inspired by this, artists in Provence began featuring cicadas in their creations, from pottery and souvenirs to paintings and sculptures.
Poet Frederic Mistral further strengthened this regional identity with his well-known phrase, “the sun makes me sing.”
Today, cicadas appear everywhere in Provence, reminding people to embrace life’s simple pleasures and to keep the light-filled spirit of summer alive all year long.
Unit 03 Reading 2 웨이터들이 쟁반을 들고 달리면 안 되는 경주?
On March 24, 2024, more than 200 waiters and waitresses gathered near Paris City Hall for the Waiters’ Race, Course des Cafés.
This exciting race celebrates the elegance and skill of French service.
Each participant carried a tray with a croissant, a glass of water, and an empty coffee cup, walking with quick yet graceful steps.
Participants raced through a 2-kilometer course with one goal: to cross the finish line as quickly as possible without running.
They were judged on their speed, how much liquid they spilled, and whether they managed to keep their dishes unbroken.
The men’s winner finished in 13 minutes and 30 seconds, while the women’s winner completed the race in 14 minutes and 12 seconds.
Each of the winners received a medal, two tickets to the Paris Olympic opening ceremony, and a one-night stay at a luxurious Paris hotel.
More than just a fun competition, the Waiters’ Race honors the 300-year history of Parisian cafés and restaurants, widely recognized as the birthplace of modern cafés and restaurants.
Parisian waiters have been at the heart of this history, setting the standard for elegant and traditional dining service.
The race not only celebrates their skill and dedication but also the proud legacy of Parisian dining culture.
Unit 03 Reading 3 왜 우리는 불쾌한 냄새에 끌릴까?
Titan arum, known as the corpse flower, releases a smell that resembles a mix of rotten fish, waste, and decaying bodies.
Although the odor is famously unpleasant, many people visit the flower to experience the smell for themselves.
Likewise, many people intentionally expose themselves to other bad smells, such as the damp scent of a basement or the earthy odor of a farm.
But why would anyone be drawn to odors that are so unpleasant?
The answer can be found in psychology.
People enjoy discomfort when it occurs in a safe and controlled situation — a phenomenon known as “benign masochism.”
Such a tendency is clear when we see people enjoying watching horror movies or eating spicy food, despite the physical or emotional discomfort involved.
Riding a roller coaster is another example: your mind knows you’re safe, but your body reacts as if you’re in danger — and that contrast creates a sense of excitement.
Another possible explanation is the “Proust effect.”
Smell is closely tied to memory and can bring up strong emotional responses.
Even an unpleasant odor, when tied to a pleasant memory, can trigger positive emotions.

For instance, the scent of an old basement might evoke memories of exploring their grandparents’ attic, while the smell of livestock odors might bring back memories of childhood visits to the countryside.
In such cases, these smells, though unpleasant, can be strangely comforting and even enjoyable.
Unit 04 Reading 1 나무들이 서로 거리를 두는 이유는?
Look up the next time you’re in a forest, and you might notice something extraordinary.
In some trees, the tops of their branches avoid contact, creating neat, puzzle-like patterns in the sky.
This fascinating natural phenomenon is called crown shyness.
Crown shyness offers significant advantages to both individual trees and the forest as a whole.
With gaps formed between branches, sunlight can reach lower branches and the forest floor, thereby enhancing photosynthesis and promoting plant growth.
In addition, these openings facilitate the flow of rainwater to the ground, keeping the soil moist and creating habitats for smaller plants and animals.

Scientists are still studying whether crown shyness is driven by external forces, like branches colliding in strong winds, or by a survival strategy, such as ensuring fair distribution of resources and limiting the spread of disease.
Although the mysteries remain, this natural process undoubtedly contributes to a thriving ecosystem.
It is clear evidence of nature’s remarkable ability to maintain delicate balance and harmony.
Unit 04 Reading 2 내가 좋아하는 정보만 쏙쏙?
Search engines are powerful tools that make finding information quick and easy.
However, they sometimes create “filter bubbles,” which limit what we see by prioritizing results based on our past interests.
Over time, this can narrow our perspective and keep us in a cycle where we only encounter ideas that we’ve accepted before.
For example, if a person frequently searches for budget-friendly travel tips, their search engine will prioritize affordable destinations and low-cost vacation ideas in future searches.
Even if they want to explore luxury options, those results might be harder to find.
Similarly, if someone searches for a specific political stance, the search engine is likely to keep presenting that side of the argument, hiding other important perspectives.
This narrowing of information makes it impossible for people to see things from various angles and make well-informed decisions.
While search engines make our lives easier, this convenience comes at a cost.
We need to stay cautious about how search engines shape the information we see.
By being aware of the limitations of personalized results, we can avoid being misled and trapped in our own biases.
Unit 04 Reading 3 이민이 가장 쉬웠어요
Svalbard, a remote island group in the Arctic Ocean, is located about 800 km north of mainland Norway.
Svalbard is full of superlatives.
It has the world’s northernmost town, university, and church.
Most importantly, it is one of the easiest places in the world to immigrate to.
Thanks to the Svalbard Treaty, citizens of 46 countries can settle here without obtaining a visa.
As long as you have a job and a place to live, you are welcome — and everyone is treated equally.
Living in Svalbard comes with unique advantages.
The island’s tax-free status makes it a financially attractive place to live and work.
Its beautiful natural environment offers thrilling activities like dog sledding.
Adding to its charm is its lively multicultural atmosphere, where residents connect with people from around the world and share a variety of experiences.
Living in Svalbard, however, does come with challenges.
The extreme climate, months of polar night, and limited infrastructure — like only 40 km of paved roads — make daily life difficult.
The local hospital lacks childbirth facilities, and burials are not allowed because the permafrost blocks natural decomposition of bodies.
Despite these difficulties, Svalbard’s breathtaking Arctic beauty and its peaceful lifestyle make it a unique destination for those seeking a fresh start.
Would you want to experience life at the edge of the world?
Unit 05 Reading 1 박테리아를 입는다고요?
Imagine a fabric that is strong, flexible, eco-friendly, and created with the help of bacteria!
Modern Synthesis, a UK-based company, is using bacteria to make new materials for clothing that don’t require animals or plastic.
This is a new step toward making fashion better for the planet.
The process starts with bacteria taken from kombucha, a fermented tea.
The bacteria are fed sugar, which they use to produce cellulose, a natural material found in plant materials like cotton and wood.
Afterward, the cellulose is processed into super-strong fibers that are then made into fabric.
This fabric can be even stronger than steel at the fiber level!
What makes this fabric special is that it can handle any style.
It is not only strong but also flexible, which makes it perfect for modern fashion.
Designers can add bright colors, fun patterns, and creative textures.
The fabric works for all kinds of styles, from minimalist designs to bold, eye-catching creations.
This innovative fabric proves that protecting the environment doesn’t mean giving up on style.
It’s an exciting glimpse into the future of green fashion!
Unit 05 Reading 2 지도에는 없는 이상한 도로들
Roads are expanding at the fastest pace in human history.
Among them are “ghost roads” — illegally constructed paths in rainforests.
These roads provide unauthorized access to untouched forests and are becoming increasingly common in the Asia-Pacific region.
Loggers, miners, and land grabbers use these roads to cut down trees and harvest valuable resources.
As a result, ghost roads are strongly linked to deforestation.
Recently, researchers and volunteers in Australia used satellite images to map these hidden roads in tropical forests across Borneo, Sumatra, and New Guinea.
They discovered 1.37 million kilometers of roads.
That is three to seven times more than what is officially recorded.
Since these roads do not appear on maps, they are extremely difficult to monitor or control.
This issue is not limited to the Asia-Pacific tropics and similar patterns have been found before in places like Cameroon, the Solomon Islands, and Brazil.
The impact of ghost roads extends well beyond deforestation.
They disrupt entire ecosystems by destroying habitats and making it harder for forests to support wildlife.
Furthermore, they weaken forests’ ability to regulate the climate.
If ghost roads continue to spread, the damage to rainforests — and to the planet — may become irreversible.
Unit 05 Reading 3 위태롭게 서 있는 바위가 하는 일
Precariously balanced rocks (PBRs) are amazing natural formations that are found in many places around the world.
These rocks are balanced in strange, or seemingly impossible positions.
For example, Bubble Rock in Maine, U.S., sits right near the edge of a cliff.
Another is Omak Rock in Washington State, which rests delicately on a thin foundation.
These unusual rocks are shaped by various natural forces over thousands of years.
Some may have been formed by glaciers, which carried massive rocks and left them in odd positions as the ice melted.
Others may have been shaped as wind and water slowly wore away the bottom of the rock until only a narrow base remained.
PBRs are interesting to look at, but they are also valuable for assessing ground stability.
By analyzing how long these rocks have remained in place without falling, scientists can learn about the region’s earthquake history.
This data is used to create more accurate earthquake hazard maps.
It can also guide decisions about where to build critical structures, such as power plants and dams, in the most stable locations.
Unit 06 Reading 1 10만 장의 반 고흐를 그린 화가
For 20 years, Zhao Xiaoyong worked as a copy artist in Dafen Village, China.
This village is well-known for its artists who replicate masterpieces.
Zhao was among the most skilled, producing over 100,000 copies of Van Gogh’s paintings.
His talent brought him steady work, but as the years passed, Zhao felt something important was missing.
The turning point came when Zhao traveled to Amsterdam and saw Van Gogh’s original paintings for the first time.
The dynamic colors, energy, and the raw emotion of the originals overwhelmed him.
In that moment, Zhao realized that he could never truly replicate the passion and spirit of Van Gogh’s work.
When Zhao returned to Dafen, he made a bold decision: no longer would he paint as Van Gogh, but as Zhao Xiaoyong.
He began creating original works that expressed his own perspective and emotions.
With each piece he painted, the emptiness he once felt slowly faded away.
His works soon began to draw attention from collectors and galleries.
Zhao gradually transformed from a copyist into a true artist.
The message in Zhao’s story is clear: true art begins with finding your own voice.
And just as important, it’s never too late to start your own artistic journey.
Unit 06 Reading 2 '카마 무타'의 감정을 느껴보았나요?
Have you ever felt goosebumps or a warmth in your chest while witnessing an act of love or devotion — like a superhero sacrificing himself or a soldier reuniting with his family?
That powerful feeling has a name you might not know: kama muta.
This ancient Sanskrit phrase, meaning ‘moved by love,’ describes the emotions we feel in such heartwarming moments.
So how is kama muta different from being ‘moved?’
Although both emotions arise from touching experiences, kama muta is unique because it’s all about connection and togetherness.
To put it in perspective, you might feel ‘moved’ by the beauty of nature or an inspiring piece of music.
Kama muta, however, is more likely to appear in moments of human connection or compassion — like witnessing someone helping a stranger or sharing their last bit of food.
It’s a feeling of genuine love, kindness, and belonging that reminds us that we’re part of something bigger — like a family, a community, or even the world around us.
Unit 06 Reading 3 공짜로 살게 해드립니다
Japan has come up with a creative idea to solve the problem of declining populations in small towns: the Zero Yen Vacant Home Bank.
This program offers empty homes to new residents at no cost.

It’s a win for everyone involved: house owners can avoid taking care of and paying fees for houses they don’t need anymore, new residents get a free place to live, and towns can welcome fresh energy into their communities.
Kamiichi, a small town in central Japan, is a good example of how the program works.
Like many rural areas in Japan, it has faced population decline as younger residents move away, whereas older ones remain.
In 2023, the town provided 13 homes through the Zero Yen Vacant Home Bank.
The program also offered financial support for moving, home repair, and childcare on condition that the applicants move into the town.
The program drew strong interest, even from overseas, and the homes were quickly taken.
For the first time in over a decade, the town saw hope to reverse its population decline.
While the program alone may not provide a permanent solution to population decline, it is bringing attention and hope to struggling towns.
Hopefully, more innovative ideas like this will breathe new life into these neighborhoods.
Unit 07 Reading 1 바느질하는 새가 있다고요?
Have you ever heard of a bird that can sew?
It’s called the tailorbird, a songbird found in Asia.
These tiny birds are about 10–14 cm long, weigh just 6–10 grams, and have bright green or grey feathers.
The bird gets its name from its remarkable ability to stitch leaves together to build its nest.
The process of building their nest begins with the female selecting fresh, strong leaves and folding them into a cup shape.
Using her beak like a needle, she makes tiny holes along the edges.
Then, she weaves plant fibers or silk from insects through the holes with her beak, just like sewing.
Meanwhile, the male gathers soft materials — such as grass, feathers, and animal hair — and lines the inner nest with them to help keep the eggs warm.
Once the nest is complete, it becomes a safe shelter in which the chicks can stay hidden from predators.
Inside, the female lays 3–5 eggs, and both parents care for the chicks until they are strong enough to leave.
Afterward, the nest is left behind and might be reused by other tailorbird pairs.
This clever nest-building strategy is crucial for protecting their young and for the survival of the tailorbird.
Unit 07 Reading 2 교도소에 고양이를 풀어놓으면 생기는 일
In a prison in Indiana, U.S., a unique program is transforming lives.
Since its start in 2015, the program has brought shelter cats — often abandoned or abused — into the prison to live alongside prisoners.
These unlikely companions are creating positive change in ways no one could have imagined.
The program benefits both prisoners and cats.
For prisoners, caring for the cats — feeding, grooming, and even knitting their clothes — gives them a sense of purpose.
It also provides comfort and companionship, sometimes for the first time in their lives.
The cats, in turn, learn to trust people again.
They get healthier, more playful, and ready for adoption under the love and care of the prisoners.
For many prisoners, the program is more than emotional support.
It teaches meaningful social skills like patience and responsibility, helping them better understand how to form positive relationships.
Most importantly, it helps them develop respect for life.
By the time they leave prison, they will have been better prepared to adapt to society.
In a place defined by strict rules and steel bars, both the abandoned cats and the prisoners find warmth, connection, and a second chance together.
They are proof that healing and growth can happen even in the most unexpected places.
Unit 07 Reading 3 건들면 깨져버릴 거예요!
In the late 1840s, Princess Alexandra Amelie of Bavaria was convinced that her body contained glass.
She believed she had swallowed a whole glass piano as a child and moved carefully, as if it were about to break at any moment.
This peculiar belief was known as “the glass delusion,” a psychological condition in which individuals believed their bodies or parts of them were fragile glass.
Many royals and nobles throughout history shared the same delusion.
The first recorded case was in the Middle Ages, and the condition became more common in the 16th and 17th centuries.
One famous case was King Charles VI of France.
He believed that his body was entirely made of glass and, to avoid breaking, he would stay still for hours, wrapped in thick blankets.
Others believed they had glass hearts, feet, or heads; one royal even thought he was a glass vase.
Doctors at the time struggled to explain the cause of this delusion.
Some linked it to depression common among nobles.
Psychologists today suggest it revealed how vulnerable and exposed they felt in their highly public roles, along with a desire to escape their pressures.
Additionally, the idea of glass as a rare and precious material, often found in palaces, likely reinforced the delusion.
Unit 08 Reading 1 비둘기가 훈장을 받은 이유
Pigeons may not be the most welcomed animals today, but during World War I, they were crucial to military communication.
When other methods failed, these birds carried life-saving messages.
One remarkable pigeon, Cher Ami — whose name means “dear friend” in French — became famous for his incredible bravery.
Cher Ami was trained by the U.S. Army as one of 600 pigeons used to deliver messages during battles.
Having completed several successful missions, Cher Ami took on his most important mission during a critical battle in 1918.
A team of troops was trapped behind enemy lines and was accidentally being bombed by their own side.
Under heavy fire and out of radio range, they had no way to call for help.
A soldier tied a message to Cher Ami’s leg, which pleaded for the bombing to stop.
Cher Ami flew through intense gunfire and, despite being shot in the chest, managed to deliver the message that saved 194 men.
After the war, Cher Ami returned to the U.S. and was awarded a medal for bravery.
He died in 1919 from his wounds, but his courage is remembered to this day.
His body is displayed at a historical museum in Washington, D.C., reminding us that these overlooked animals were once war-time heroes.
Unit 08 Reading 2 일할 때 이것도 중요해요
People often switch jobs for better salaries or career opportunities.
However,   a growing number of workers are resigning because their companies fail to take environmental issues seriously.
These individuals are called “climate quitters.”
One example is Steffen Krutzinna, an energy trader from Germany.
When Shell, his company’s parent company, abandoned its climate goals to cut oil production, he decided to leave immediately.
He believed that working for a company that did not share his environmental values was no longer an option.
Recent studies indicate that this trend is rising as public awareness of climate issues grows.
A survey in the UK found that 35% of employees were willing to quit their jobs if their company lacked strong green policies.
Among younger generations, such as Gen Z workers, this number rose to 53%.
A related finding was that employees tend to be more satisfied and have higher retention rates in companies that prioritize sustainable practices.
On the other hand, some experts believe that quitting isn’t the only option.
They advise that staying and pushing their companies to commit to climate efforts can yield greater benefits for both employees and companies.
The rise of climate quitters shows the growing role of climate concerns in workplace decisions.
As this movement continues, businesses may need to adapt by integrating sustainable practices in order to attract and retain skilled workers.
Unit 08 Reading 3 SOS는 원래 무슨 뜻일까?
For over 100 years, SOS has been a universal call for help.
Yet, few people know what it actually stands for.
Many believe it means “Save Our Ship” or “Save Our Souls,” but in fact, it doesn’t stand for anything!
Back in 1906, SOS was chosen because it’s easy to recognize in Morse code: three dots (···), three dashes (–––), and three dots (···) again.
Before SOS became the international emergency signal, countries used their own codes.
The British used “CQD,” which meant “Come Quickly, Distress.”
Germans used “SOE,” and Italians had “SSSDDD.”
These signals often caused confusion and delay because they were all different and required pauses between letters.
To fix this, experts created SOS — a fast and simple universal signal.
The first official use of SOS was in 1909, when the ship RMS Slavonia sent the signal after hitting rocks near the Azores.
The clear message allowed rescue ships to locate and save passengers effectively.
A few years later, the Titanic used both “SOS” and “CQD” during its sinking in 1912.
Although help arrived too late to save many lives, the tragedy made SOS universally famous as the call for help.
Over time, SOS became more than a code — it became a symbol of an urgent need for help.
Today, SOS is instantly recognized no matter how it is sent — through radio waves, messages in the sand, or signals of light.
Unit 09 Reading 1 못생기면 유죄라고?
In 19th and 20th century America, looking different was treated as a crime.
In 1867, San Francisco passed some unusual and cruel laws known as the ‘ugly laws.’
These laws banned people who were considered ‘unpleasant to look at’ from appearing in public.
Similar laws soon spread to other major cities, targeting individuals with visible disabilities or illnesses.
During this time, American cities experienced rapid growth and public spaces became increasingly crowded.
Maintaining order and preserving a ‘pleasing’ urban environment became a priority for city officials.
The ugly laws were based on the belief that people with visible differences somehow damaged the city’s image.
Life was incredibly difficult for those affected by ugly laws.
They had to face severe social isolation, often losing their jobs and their means of financial support.
Many were forced out of public spaces and deprived of essential social and economic opportunities.
Tragically, these laws remained in effect for nearly 100 years.
This shameful chapter in history later became a powerful example for disability rights activists.
It was used to highlight the unfair discrimination faced by people with disabilities.
The activists’ persistent fight for justice led to the Americans with Disabilities Act in 1990, a law that protects the rights of people with disabilities.
It’s upsetting to look back on the harsh history of the ‘ugly laws,’ but it provides a crucial lesson about the need for equality for all people.
Unit 09 Reading 2 한 마리만 키우면 불법
If you’re serious about animal rights, Switzerland’s laws may impress you.
In 2008, the country passed a law making it illegal to own just one guinea pig.
This law was introduced because guinea pigs naturally live in groups.
Without companions to interact with, they would suffer from stress and depression.
The law even considers cases where one guinea pig lives longer than the other — owners can rent another pig so the remaining one has company until it passes away.
Of course, guinea pigs aren’t the only animals protected under these pioneering laws.
All social animals, including rabbits, birds, and goldfish, are required to have at least one companion.
Cats, though they are allowed to be kept alone, must still have opportunities to see or socialize with other cats, such as through a window or in shared spaces.
Dog owners are also required to let their dogs have regular contact with humans and fellow dogs.
These regulations prove Switzerland’s strong commitment to animal rights, with it being the first country to formally recognize the concept of social rights for animals.
Unit 09 Reading 3 지름신은 이제 나를 못 속여!
In a world where shopping hauls and unboxing videos flood social media, many people feel the pressure to keep up with fast fashion trends and buy things they don’t truly need.
I used to be one of them, constantly purchasing clothes, gadgets, and beauty products.
But over time, I began to question these habits.
Now, I take pride in making intentional choices and practicing underconsumption.
I adopted underconsumption after realizing how much unnecessary stuff I had accumulated.
My closet was packed with barely worn clothes, and my drawers held forgotten beauty products that had expired.
I couldn’t believe how much money I had wasted!
On top of that, many of these excess items eventually end up in landfills, contributing to environmental pollution.
Rather than chasing the latest trends, I now focus on fully utilizing what I already own.
I repair old clothes instead of replacing them, find new uses for household items, and make sure to use things up before considering a new purchase.
My mindset has shifted — I no longer buy something just because it’s on sale or trending.
When I do need something, I carefully consider its necessity and look for secondhand options first.
Practicing underconsumption has helped me live a simpler and more mindful life while also reducing my environmental impact.
I’m glad to know that my choices make a positive difference in my life and the world around me.
Unit 10 Reading 1 껌 한 개가 신발이 되기까지
Discarded chewing gum is a big problem for many cities around the world.
In the UK alone, local governments spend around $82 million each year to clean chewed gum off sidewalks.
But one designer, Anna Bullus, came up with a creative idea to solve this sticky problem.
While studying design, Anna realized that gum is made from synthetic rubber and shares some qualities with plastic.
That gave her an idea: if gum is like plastic, why don’t we recycle it the same way?
She developed a special process to mix gum with other recycled materials to create plastic pellets.
These pellets can be used in regular plastic-making machines and turned into everyday items like combs, frisbees, and reusable coffee mugs.
One of the most exciting inventions from her recycling idea is the Gumshoe sneaker.
These sneakers have soles made from a material that includes 20% recycled gum.
They come in playful colors like bubblegum pink and even smell like bubblegum!
They are produced by Gumdrop, a company Anna founded to tackle gum waste.
In the coming years, Gumdrop will be turning discarded gum into a valuable resource while helping to clean the streets.
It’s a smart way to transform a sticky problem into something practical — and even stylish!
Unit 10 Reading 2 같은 날, 두 개의 이름
Every October, the United States observes a holiday on the second Monday of the month.
Traditionally, this day has been called Columbus Day, celebrating Christopher Columbus’s arrival in the Americas in 1492.
However, many have raised questions about whether the name of the holiday is appropriate.
They point out that Columbus’s arrival led to the colonization and suffering of native peoples who had lived in the Americas for thousands of years.
In 1977, Native American leaders proposed changing the holiday’s name to Indigenous Peoples’ Day to honor the heritage of native communities.
Over time, more than 100 cities, along with several states like California, Alaska, and Oregon, have adopted this new name.
Even former President Biden officially recognized Indigenous Peoples’ Day in 2021.
For Italian Americans, Columbus Day holds a different meaning.
Since Columbus was born in Genoa, Italy, they view the day as a celebration of Italian heritage and pride.
Some suggest renaming it Italian Heritage Day to reflect this.
In cities like New York, both Indigenous Peoples’ Day and Italian Heritage Day are observed on the same date.
Whether you call it Columbus Day, Indigenous Peoples’ Day, or something else, the holiday continues to spark important conversations about American history, culture, and identity.
What do you think it should be called?
Unit 10 Reading 3 아픈 침팬지는 무엇을 먹을까?
What if wild animals knew more about medicine than we thought?
In Uganda’s Budongo Forest, chimpanzees have been observed eating plants — possibly to heal their injuries or illnesses.
Researchers from the University of Oxford studied 51 wild chimpanzees from two communities in the forest.
Some chimps that appeared to be injured were seen eating plants that were not part of their usual diet.
For instance, a chimpanzee with an injured hand chewed on leaves from a certain plant, while another with a parasitic infection consumed the bark of a certain thorn tree.
The researchers collected samples from 13 plant species that the sick chimps had eaten.
When these samples were tested in the laboratory, most were found to have strong healing properties.
The leaves the chimps ate were shown to reduce pain and swelling, while the bark exhibited powerful antibacterial effects.
Some plants were so effective at treating wounds and illnesses that local East African communities also used them for cuts, stomach problems, and even snake bites.
This finding provides strong evidence that chimpanzees might be using plants for self-medication.
It provides insight into the exceptional intelligence of these animals and opens new possibilities for developing natural medicines for humans.
Unit 11 Reading 1 하늘에 떠 있는 코끼리 100마리
When you look at the clouds, they appear light and fluffy, like cotton candy drifting across the sky.
But don’t be fooled — clouds are much heavier than they seem.
An average cumulus cloud weighs around 550 tons, or about the same as 100 elephants!
So, how do these enormous clouds stay in the sky?
Clouds are made of incredibly tiny water particles, each about a million times smaller than a raindrop.
These particles are widely spread out and mixed with a large amount of air, which explains the cloud’s containing far more air than water.
As a result, the cloud’s overall density is lower than the surrounding large volume of air.
This allows the cloud to float.
Warm air rising from the ground also lifts the cloud higher, while wind currents keep the water particles moving.
These factors altogether prevent the water particles from falling until they gather and grow heavy enough to fall as rain.
While all clouds share the ability to float, their structures and compositions are not all the same.
Light cirrus clouds hold less water and are easier to keep in the sky, whereas thunderclouds carry so much water that they are harder to hold up.
Nevertheless, all clouds stay in the sky thanks to the same natural factors — air density, rising warm air, and wind — working together in perfect harmony.
Unit 11 Reading 2 비가 쏟아지는데 물이 없다니
In the hills of northeastern India lies Cherrapunji, a village described as one of the wettest places on Earth.
It receives an average annual rainfall of 11,430 mm — about as much as South Korea gets over ten years!
This extreme rainfall creates a green landscape, misty hills, and spectacular waterfalls that attract visitors from around the world.
But here’s the strange part: despite all this heavy rain, Cherrapunji faces serious water shortages.
This is due to a mix of complex issues.
Most of the rain falls within a short monsoon season, and the village’s steep, rocky landscape causes the rainwater to flow away quickly instead of soaking into the ground.
In addition, deforestation has greatly reduced the number of trees, which makes it harder for the soil to hold water.
Climate change has also made things worse by causing longer dry periods and rising temperatures.
These water shortages cause real problems for the people of Cherrapunji.
During the dry months, there is often not enough water for drinking, farming, or daily use.
Many villagers must walk long distances or pay high prices to get it.
Some experts call Cherrapunji a “wet desert” to highlight the bitter irony of its situation.
Hopefully, this unique village will discover solutions and ensure a sustainable future for its people.
Unit 11 Reading 3 소리 없이도 대화가 넘치는 마을
Sandi was born deaf, just like many in his family.
He cannot hear, but in his village, that has never once been a problem.
Everyone in his school learns a special sign language, and the entire village communicates using it.
This is a story of Bengkala, a small village in Bali, Indonesia.
Among its 3,000 residents, 44 are deaf due to a genetic condition passed down for seven generations.
But unlike in many places, where deafness can lead to isolation, Bengkala has built a community where everyone can interact without barriers.
The villagers developed Kata Kolok, which is their own sign language.
It is a fully independent language with its own grammar, structure, and vocabulary.
Kata Kolok is spoken only in Bengkala and is used by both deaf and hearing villagers.
Around 80 percent of the community understands and uses it, ensuring that everyone, regardless of their ability to hear, can fully participate in village life.
Everyday interactions in Bengkala happen effortlessly in sign language.
Deaf and hearing villagers chat casually, children play games using gestures, and community meetings are conducted in signing.
Here, signing is not just a language — it is a bridge that unites the villagers.
The story of Bengkala demonstrates the power of shared language in building a truly inclusive society.
When communication is accessible to everyone, connection thrives, and no one is left behind.
Unit 12 Reading 1 책을 숨겨 나른 낙원의 길
The Panemune road, often called Lithuania’s “paradise road,” winds through over 100 kilometers of breathtaking scenery.
But this road is more than just beautiful — it played a major role in protecting the Lithuanian language.
In the late 1800s, Lithuania was ruled by Russia, and the Lithuanian language was banned.
Printing, selling, or even owning Lithuanian texts became illegal.
Yet, many brave people resisted by smuggling books.
Nearly 40,000 Lithuanian books were published abroad and secretly brought into Lithuania, with the Panemune road being a main route for this work.
Smuggling books was extremely dangerous.
Smugglers hid books in hay, furniture, and coffins, and took a life-threatening journey on the road.
If discovered, they could be shot or sent to prison, where they were tortured or executed.
Despite the risks, people from all backgrounds — farmers, priests, doctors, and many more — came together to form a large and effective network.
Their efforts continued for 39 years until their network became so strong that the Russian authorities could no longer stop them.
In 1904, the ban on the Lithuanian language was removed and the language was brought back to life.
Today, every year on March 16, Lithuania celebrates the Day of the Book Smugglers to honor those who risked everything to preserve the Lithuanian language and identity.
The Panemune road, once walked by these heroes, stands as a silent witness to their unbreakable spirit.
Unit 12 Reading 2 고등학생이 만든 50개 별 국기
The current American flag has a fascinating origin — it all started with a high school project.
In 1958, the United States had only 48 states, but there was a possibility that Alaska and Hawaii would soon join the Union.
Seventeen-year-old Robert Heft decided to redesign the flag as part of a school project, with the hope that the two states would officially join soon.
Robert spent over 12 hours creating a 50-star flag.
He carefully cut out stars, arranged them into neat rows, and stitched them onto the 48-star flag.
But when Heft presented his flag at school, his teacher was dissatisfied.
The teacher said, “You don’t even know how many states we have!”
and gave him a B- grade.
Robert was determined to prove the value of his design, so he wrote letters to the White House and asked them to consider his flag.
Two years later, after Alaska and Hawaii officially became American states, the president of the United States called Robert with thrilling news: his flag design had been chosen.
On July 4, 1960, Robert was invited to see the flag-raising ceremony at the U.S. Capitol, where his 50-star flag was raised for the first time.
Robert’s flag remains the longest-used flag design in U.S. history.
He even prepared a 51-star version.
If another state should join the Union, his new design would be ready.
Unit 12 Reading 3 깨진 광고판이 대박 상품이 된 이유
In 2023, during a baseball game in New York, superstar Shohei Ohtani hit a foul ball that smashed an advertisement panel for Coors Light, a popular beer brand in the U.S.
The broken pixels left a black box above the logo on the Coors Light’s silver can.
The flaw could have been a marketing disaster.
But Coors Light took a daring approach.
They chose not to hide the flaw, but to spotlight it.
Within 48 hours, they released a limited-edition can featuring the black square above the brand’s logo.
This quickly went viral on social media.
Fans loved the playful design, and the cans sold out in less than a day.
Some fans, disappointed by the sellout, went as far as to draw black squares on their regular cans.
Even the broken panel itself became a popular souvenir and was auctioned for over 7,000 dollars!
What made the idea so successful?
Coors Light embraced their embarrassment in a self-aware and humorous way, which connected strongly with fans.
And rather than relying on expensive or complex strategies, they simply used their situation swiftly and naturally to their advantage.
This clever campaign not only saved the moment but elevated Coors Light’s image.
Creating a marketing masterpiece isn’t always about a massive budget — sometimes, it is just a broken ad and a sense of humor that leave a lasting impression.
